lit: small heart, reverent and respectful: acting with a careful, watchful heart

story.text: The phrase comes from the Book of Songs, in an ode praising King Wen of Zhou, who is described as xiaoxin yiyi: careful and reverent. There it described his respectful conduct in serving Heaven. Over time the sense shifted, and today it simply means doing something with great caution.

use.how: Usually an adverbial with 地 before a verb (小心翼翼地走) or a predicate. Describes how a person handles something fragile, risky or sensitive.

near.diff: 一丝不苟 praises meticulous attention to standards and detail; 小心翼翼 is caution for fear of breaking, falling or offending.

cue: Carrying a full bowl of hot soup across a crowded room, step by step, eyes fixed on it. How does she walk?

ctx.s: 妈妈{小心翼翼}地把蛋糕从盒子里拿了出来。
ctx.en: Mum took the cake out of the box very carefully.

ctx.s: 地上结了冰，大家都{小心翼翼}地往前走。
ctx.en: The ground was icy, so everyone moved forward very cautiously.

ctx.s: 他第一次抱刚出生的女儿，动作{小心翼翼}的。
ctx.en: Holding his newborn daughter for the first time, he moved with great care.

ctx.s: “你说话怎么这么{小心翼翼}？”“我怕说错话惹老板生气。”
ctx.en: "Why are you choosing your words so carefully?" "I'm afraid of saying something that will annoy the boss."

ctx.s: 自从上次被骗以后，她跟陌生人打交道总是{小心翼翼}。
ctx.en: Since she was cheated last time, she has always been very wary in dealing with strangers.

ctx.s: 谈判的时候，双方都{小心翼翼}地避开了价格问题。
ctx.en: During the negotiation, both sides carefully steered clear of the question of price.

bad.s: {小心翼翼}！后面有车开过来了！
bad.en: (meant: Look out! There's a car coming up behind you!)
bad.why: It describes the careful manner in which someone does something; it cannot be shouted as a warning. To warn someone, say xiaoxin (look out).

bad.s: 这个计划写得很{小心翼翼}。
bad.en: (meant: this plan was written thoroughly)
bad.why: It describes a person's cautious manner, not the quality of a document. A thorough plan is zhoumi (well thought out) or xiangxi (detailed).

lit: a coarse heart and a big, loose mind

use.how: A predicate or attributive (太粗心大意了，粗心大意的人). Criticises carelessness that causes a mistake, often in work, exams or driving.

near.diff: 丢三落四 is the habit of forgetting or losing belongings; 粗心大意 is carelessness in doing a task, which leads to errors.
心不在焉 is having one's mind elsewhere at the moment; 粗心大意 is not taking enough care, whatever the reason.

cue: A student knew every answer but lost marks for copying a number wrong and skipping the last page. What went wrong?

ctx.s: 考试的时候千万别{粗心大意}，写完要检查一遍。
ctx.en: Whatever you do, don't be careless in the exam; check everything once you've finished.

ctx.s: 他太{粗心大意}了，把“己”字写成了“已”字。
ctx.en: He was so careless that he wrote the character ji (self) as yi (already).

ctx.s: 这次事故是司机一时{粗心大意}造成的。
ctx.en: This accident was caused by a moment's carelessness on the driver's part.

ctx.s: “又算错了？”“对不起，我太{粗心大意}了。”
ctx.en: "Wrong again?" "Sorry, I was too careless."

ctx.s: 做实验可不能{粗心大意}，一个数据错了，结果就全错了。
ctx.en: You can't be careless in an experiment: one wrong figure and the whole result is wrong.

ctx.s: 合同里有一个数字写错了，都怪他{粗心大意}。
ctx.en: A figure in the contract was written wrongly, all because of his carelessness.

bad.s: 作业很简单，我{粗心大意}地做完了，得了满分。
bad.en: (meant: I finished the easy homework without effort and got full marks)
bad.why: It means careless and blames someone for errors; it cannot mean relaxed or effortless, and clashes with a perfect result.

bad.s: 这道题很{粗心大意}。
bad.en: (meant: this question is tricky and easy to get wrong)
bad.why: Only a person can be careless. For a tricky question, say it is easy to get wrong (rongyi chucuo).

lit: to lose three and leave four behind

use.how: A predicate or attributive about a person's habit (他总是丢三落四的). It takes no object: you cannot 丢三落四 a particular thing.

near.diff: 粗心大意 is carelessness that causes mistakes in a task; 丢三落四 is specifically forgetting or losing one's things, again and again.

cue: Your brother leaves his keys at home, his umbrella on the bus and his homework on the kitchen table, every single week. What is he like?

ctx.s: 我弟弟总是{丢三落四}的，今天又把作业忘在家里了。
ctx.en: My little brother is always forgetting things; today he left his homework at home again.

ctx.s: 你怎么这么{丢三落四}？雨伞都丢了三把了！
ctx.en: How can you be so forgetful? You've already lost three umbrellas!

ctx.s: 年纪大了，我也开始{丢三落四}，出门老是忘带手机。
ctx.en: Now that I'm older, I've started forgetting things too; I'm always going out without my phone.

ctx.s: 出发前列一张清单，就不会{丢三落四}了。
ctx.en: Make a list before you set off and you won't leave things behind.

ctx.s: 她以前很{丢三落四}，现在出门前都要把包检查一遍。
ctx.en: She used to lose things all the time; now she checks her bag before she goes out.

ctx.s: 像他这样{丢三落四}的人，最好别让他保管护照。
ctx.en: Someone as forgetful as him had better not be put in charge of the passports.

bad.s: 我今天把钥匙{丢三落四}了。
bad.en: (meant: I lost my keys today)
bad.why: It describes a habit and takes no object. To say you lost your keys, use the plain verb diu (to lose).

bad.s: 搬家前他{丢三落四}，扔了很多旧东西。
bad.en: (meant: before moving he got rid of lots of old things)
bad.why: It is about forgetting or losing things by accident, not deliberately throwing them away.

use.how: A predicate or adverbial with 地, often 对…半信半疑. The subject is the person who hears something and is unsure whether it is true.

near.diff: 犹豫不决 is being unable to decide what to do; 半信半疑 is being unsure whether what one hears is true.

cue: A friend tells you the shop is giving away free phones today. It sounds too good to be true, but maybe it is real. How do you take the news?

ctx.s: 听说明天放假，同学们都{半信半疑}。
ctx.en: When they heard tomorrow was a day off, the students weren't sure whether to believe it.

ctx.s: 他说自己中了大奖，我听了{半信半疑}。
ctx.en: He said he'd won a big prize; I only half believed him.

ctx.s: 她{半信半疑}地打开那封邮件，没想到真的是录取通知。
ctx.en: Half doubting, she opened the email, and to her surprise it really was an offer of admission.

ctx.s: “这种药真的有用吗？”奶奶{半信半疑}地问医生。
ctx.en: "Does this medicine really work?" Grandma asked the doctor doubtfully.

ctx.s: 一开始大家对这个新方法{半信半疑}，用了一个月才发现效果不错。
ctx.en: At first everyone was sceptical about the new method; only after a month did they find it worked well.

ctx.s: 对网上各种减肥广告，我一直抱着{半信半疑}的态度。
ctx.en: I've always taken all those online weight-loss ads with a pinch of salt.

bad.s: 我{半信半疑}地做了一半作业就去睡觉了。
bad.en: (meant: I did half my homework and went to bed)
bad.why: Here 'half' belongs to belief and doubt; it says nothing about doing half of a task.

bad.s: 这个消息很{半信半疑}。
bad.en: (meant: this news is doubtful)
bad.why: The person who hears the news is half doubting, not the news itself. Say you half believe the news, or that it is not very credible.

lit: to know one bit and understand half

story.text: Dictionaries trace the phrase to Canglang Remarks on Poetry by the Song-dynasty critic Yan Yu. Grading poets by how deeply they had grasped the art, he distinguished a thorough understanding from one that reaches only 'one bit of knowledge and half an understanding'.

use.how: A predicate (对…一知半解) or attributive (一知半解的知识). Criticises shallow knowledge, or modestly describes one's own.

near.diff: 一窍不通 is knowing nothing at all; 一知半解 is knowing a little, superficially, often while thinking one knows more.
不懂装懂 is pretending to understand; 一知半解 describes how much one actually understands.

cue: After reading two articles online, your neighbour lectures everyone about investing, but gets the basics wrong. How much does he really understand?

ctx.s: 我对电脑只是{一知半解}，这个问题我修不了。
ctx.en: I only know a little about computers; I can't fix this problem.

ctx.s: 别看他说得头头是道，其实他对这一行{一知半解}。
ctx.en: He may sound convincing, but actually his knowledge of this trade is shallow.

ctx.s: 学东西最怕{一知半解}，以为自己懂了，其实没懂。
ctx.en: The worst thing in learning is half-understanding: thinking you've got it when you haven't.

ctx.s: “你能给我讲讲这个法律问题吗？”“我也{一知半解}，你最好去问律师。”
ctx.en: "Can you explain this legal question to me?" "I only half understand it myself; you'd better ask a lawyer."

ctx.s: 凭着{一知半解}的知识就给别人看病，太危险了。
ctx.en: Treating people's illnesses on the strength of half-baked knowledge is far too dangerous.

ctx.s: 说明书我读了两遍，懂了一部分，可还是{一知半解}。
ctx.en: I've read the instructions twice and got some of it, but I still only half understand them.

bad.s: 我对日语{一知半解}，一个字也看不懂。
bad.en: (meant: I know nothing about Japanese and can't read a word)
bad.why: It means knowing a little, not nothing. For knowing nothing at all, the idiom is yi qiao bu tong.

bad.s: 他特别聪明，老师讲一点，他就{一知半解}了。
bad.en: (meant: he's so bright he grasps the whole thing from a hint)
bad.why: It criticises shallow understanding; it is not praise for quick learning. For grasping a lot from a hint, say ju yi fan san.

mean: to know absolutely nothing about a subject
lit: not even one opening is clear: in old thought the heart had openings for understanding

use.how: A predicate, usually 对…一窍不通, about a subject or skill. Often self-deprecating (我对音乐一窍不通), or critical of someone else.

near.diff: 一知半解 is knowing a little, superficially; 一窍不通 is knowing nothing whatsoever about the subject.

cue: Someone asks you to fix their car engine. You have never opened a bonnet in your life and couldn't name a single part. What do you say?

ctx.s: 我对做饭{一窍不通}，连鸡蛋都不会煎。
ctx.en: I know nothing at all about cooking; I can't even fry an egg.

ctx.s: 他对音乐{一窍不通}，却非要当评委。
ctx.en: He knows absolutely nothing about music, yet he insists on being a judge.

ctx.s: “你懂车吗？”“我对汽车{一窍不通}，只会开。”
ctx.en: "Do you know about cars?" "I know nothing about them; I can only drive one."

ctx.s: 刚来公司的时候，我对财务{一窍不通}，全靠同事带我。
ctx.en: When I first joined the company I knew nothing about finance; I relied entirely on my colleagues to teach me.

ctx.s: 一个对法律{一窍不通}的人，怎么能当律师呢？
ctx.en: How can someone who knows nothing about law be a lawyer?

ctx.s: 爷爷原来对手机{一窍不通}，现在都会视频聊天了。
ctx.en: Grandpa used to know nothing about mobile phones; now he can even video chat.

bad.s: 前面在修路，这条路{一窍不通}。
bad.en: (meant: the road ahead is blocked by roadworks)
bad.why: It is only about knowing nothing of a subject; tong here is not 'passing through'. For a blocked road say the road is bu tong.

bad.s: 我跟新来的同事{一窍不通}，还没说过话。
bad.en: (meant: I don't know the new colleague at all)
bad.why: It is about a field of knowledge or a skill, not about knowing a person. To say you don't know someone well, say bu shu.

lit: familiarity can give birth to skill

story.text: The saying is traditionally illustrated by the tale of the oil seller. Chen Yaozi was a famous archer who hit the target eight or nine times out of ten. An old oil seller watching him only nodded slightly. When Chen asked whether his shooting was not skilled, the old man said there was no secret, only a practised hand. He set a gourd on the ground, covered its mouth with a coin with a square hole, and poured oil through the hole without wetting the coin. The four-character phrase itself is later.

use.how: Stands alone as a saying or a clause, often to encourage (多练练，熟能生巧) or to explain someone's skill. Not used as an attributive.

cue: Your nephew is frustrated that his first dumplings fall apart. You tell him that after a few hundred more, his hands will know what to do.

ctx.s: 别着急，多练几次，{熟能生巧}嘛。
ctx.en: Don't worry, practise a few more times; practice makes perfect.

ctx.s: 刚开始他包饺子很慢，后来{熟能生巧}，一分钟能包好几个。
ctx.en: At first he was slow at making dumplings, but with practice he got so good he could make several a minute.

ctx.s: 老师常说：写字没有捷径，只有{熟能生巧}。
ctx.en: The teacher often says there's no shortcut to good handwriting, only practice.

ctx.s: “你打字怎么这么快？”“天天打，{熟能生巧}呗。”
ctx.en: "How do you type so fast?" "I type every day; practice makes perfect, that's all."

ctx.s: 他做了二十年木匠，{熟能生巧}，不用尺子也能锯得很直。
ctx.en: After twenty years as a carpenter his skill is such that he can saw straight without a ruler.

ctx.s: 所谓{熟能生巧}，任何技能都要靠大量重复才能掌握。
ctx.en: As the saying goes, practice makes perfect: any skill takes a great deal of repetition to master.

bad.s: 他真是{熟能生巧}，第一次做饭就做得特别好吃。
bad.en: (meant: he's a natural; his very first meal was delicious)
bad.why: The saying credits skill to long practice, so it contradicts doing well the first time. For natural talent, say someone has tianfu (a gift).

bad.s: 我们俩认识十年了，所以{熟能生巧}。
bad.en: (meant: we've known each other ten years, so we get along well)
bad.why: Shu here means practised at a skill, not close to a person. For friends who get along, say they are hen shu or hen you moqi.

use.how: A predicate, adverbial with 地, or complement after 得 (吵得没完没了). Complains that something tiresome won't stop: rain, noise, talk, arguments.

cue: The upstairs neighbours have been drilling since eight this morning, and it is now evening. You complain to your flatmate.

ctx.s: 这雨下得{没完没了}，衣服都晾不干。
ctx.en: This rain just won't stop; the washing can't even dry.

ctx.s: 你别{没完没了}地问了，我已经回答过了！
ctx.en: Stop asking over and over; I've already answered!

ctx.s: 楼上在装修，电钻声{没完没了}，吵得我没法休息。
ctx.en: The flat upstairs is being renovated and the drilling goes on and on; I can't get any rest.

ctx.s: 一说起他的狗，他就{没完没了}。
ctx.en: Once he starts talking about his dog, there's no stopping him.

ctx.s: 会开了三个小时还{没完没了}，大家都不耐烦了。
ctx.en: The meeting had been going for three hours with no end in sight, and everyone was getting impatient.

ctx.s: 两个孩子为一个玩具吵得{没完没了}，最后妈妈把玩具收走了。
ctx.en: The two children squabbled endlessly over a toy, until Mum finally took it away.

bad.s: 这本小说太好看了，我希望它{没完没了}。
bad.en: (meant: this novel is so good I wish it would never end)
bad.why: It is a complaint about something tiresome; it cannot express a wish that something good would last.

bad.s: 他还{没完没了}作业，不能出去玩。
bad.en: (meant: he hasn't finished his homework, so he can't go out)
bad.why: It does not mean 'not yet finished' and takes no object. Say the homework is not done yet (hai mei zuowan).

mean: truly living up to its name or reputation

use.how: A predicate or attributive, very often 是名副其实的… (a true…). Confirms that a name, title or reputation matches the facts.

cue: A town calls itself the city of flowers, and when you visit, every street really is full of blossoms all year round.

ctx.s: 这里一年四季都开着花，真是{名副其实}的花城。
ctx.en: Flowers bloom here all year round; it truly deserves to be called the City of Flowers.

ctx.s: 他每天要看好几个小时的书，是个{名副其实}的书迷。
ctx.en: He reads for several hours every day; he's a bookworm in every sense of the word.

ctx.s: 都说这家店的烤鸭好吃，今天一尝，果然{名副其实}。
ctx.en: Everyone says this restaurant's roast duck is good; having tried it today, it really lives up to its reputation.

ctx.s: “这座山为什么叫雪山？”“山顶一年到头都是雪，{名副其实}嘛。”
ctx.en: "Why is this mountain called Snow Mountain?" "The peak is covered in snow all year; the name fits."

ctx.s: 这支球队连续三年拿了冠军，成了{名副其实}的强队。
ctx.en: Having won the championship three years running, the team has become a powerhouse in the true sense.

ctx.s: 大家都叫他“活字典”，什么难字他都认识，真是{名副其实}。
ctx.en: Everyone calls him a "walking dictionary", and he really does know every difficult character: the name truly fits.

bad.s: 他{名副其实}地叫王明，不是小名。
bad.en: (meant: his real name is Wang Ming, not a nickname)
bad.why: It is a judgement that a name or reputation fits the facts, not a way of saying 'real name' (zhenming).

bad.s: 她的名字很{名副其实}，听起来很美。
bad.en: (meant: her name is lovely)
bad.why: It does not mean a name sounds nice; it means the person or thing deserves its name. A nice-sounding name is hao ting.

lit: ordinary home cooking, a simple everyday meal

use.how: A noun, usually after 是 or 成了: 加班是家常便饭. Says something happens all the time, often something hard. Can still mean a simple home meal.

near.diff: 理所当然 says something is natural and to be expected; 家常便饭 says it happens so often it is routine.

cue: A firefighter shrugs when asked about being woken at three in the morning: it happens several times a week.

ctx.s: 当医生的，加班是{家常便饭}。
ctx.en: For doctors, working overtime is an everyday thing.

ctx.s: 对他来说，出差就跟{家常便饭}一样。
ctx.en: For him, business trips are completely routine.

ctx.s: 在这个城市，堵车早就成了{家常便饭}。
ctx.en: In this city, traffic jams have long been part of daily life.

ctx.s: “你们公司经常开会开到很晚吗？”“那是{家常便饭}。”
ctx.en: "Does your company often have meetings that run late?" "That happens all the time."

ctx.s: 小时候家里穷，饿肚子是{家常便饭}。
ctx.en: Our family was poor when I was little; going hungry was a regular thing.

ctx.s: 有空来我家吃顿{家常便饭}吧，不用客气。
ctx.en: Come round for a simple home-cooked meal when you're free; no need to stand on ceremony.

bad.s: 他{家常便饭}地迟到，老板很生气。
bad.en: (meant: he is late all the time and the boss is angry)
bad.why: It is a noun, not an adverb. Say that being late is a daily thing for him, or simply that he is often late.

bad.s: 去年我第一次出国，真是{家常便饭}。
bad.en: (meant: going abroad for the first time last year was a big experience)
bad.why: It means something routine and frequent, so it cannot describe a first-time, special event.
